claims.text: The target alloy has the composition Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
The target alloy is additively manufactured.
The starting microstructure is a homogeneous, single-phase fcc solid solution.
The starting surfaces and grain boundaries contain minimal preexisting oxide.
Elevated-temperature exposure in an oxidizing atmosphere produces oxide in the target alloy.
Titanium preferentially oxidizes at grain boundaries under oxidizing conditions.
Preferential titanium oxidation creates a discontinuous, brittle, Ti-rich grain-boundary oxide scale.
The Ti-rich oxide scale adheres poorly and readily spalls.
Failure or spallation of the oxide opens fast paths for oxygen ingress along grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary oxygen ingress locally depletes and embrittles the fcc matrix.
Localized grain-boundary embrittlement governs accelerated degradation and promotes catastrophic failure.
A reducing H2/N2 atmosphere suppresses formation of the deleterious Ti-rich oxide.
Suppressing the oxide maintains better intergranular cohesion and mechanical integrity.
At the same temperature and exposure time, reducing conditions will produce a thinner or more adherent oxide than oxidizing conditions.
Reducing conditions will cause less grain-boundary embrittlement than the oxidizing baseline.
Reducing conditions will improve ductility and resistance to brittle fracture and will delay or prevent catastrophic failure.
The proposed governing behavior applies around 800 degrees Celsius under atmospheres that are distinctly oxidizing or reducing.
Al and Cr may modify oxide-growth kinetics or morphology and thereby alter adhesion and degradation.
A controlled oxidizing-versus-reducing atmosphere comparison at fixed temperature, pressure, and exposure time can test the proposed mechanism.
Failure of reducing exposure to improve both oxide characteristics and mechanical integrity would falsify the proposed Ti-driven grain-boundary oxidation mechanism.
